interactions.label: In the pathogenesis of ethmoidal nasal polyps, what causes the oedematous mucosa

params.question: In the pathogenesis of ethmoidal nasal polyps, what causes the oedematous mucosa to protrude outward from the middle meatus?

answers.text: Bacterial superinfection of the oedematous ethmoid mucosa

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bacterial infection drives rhinosinusitis, not polyp formation. Polyps arise from chronic eosinophilic (type 2) inflammation, not bacterial colonisation.

answers.text: Negative pressure generated by airflow through the narrowed ostiomeatal complex

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Eosinophilic inflammation causes the mucosa to become waterlogged; airflow through the narrowed complex creates negative pressure that gradually draws the swollen lining outward to form polyps.

answers.text: Direct erosion of the lateral nasal wall by eosinophil granule proteins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While eosinophils are central to polyp pathogenesis, they do not erode bone. Bone erosion is a route by which sinus infection spreads to the orbit.

answers.text: Loss of ciliary function leading to mucus accumulation and outgrowth

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ciliary dysfunction and mucus stagnation are the pathway to rhinosinusitis, not the mechanism of polyp protrusion.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key mechanism is negative pressure. Type 2 inflammation causes mucosal oedema; airflow through the narrowed ostiomeatal complex then draws the waterlogged mucosa outward as polyps. Ciliary dysfunction and bacterial infection drive rhinosinusitis, not polyp formation.

Well done. Chronic eosinophilic inflammation causes mucosal oedema, and negative pressure from airflow through the narrowed ostiomeatal complex draws the mucosa outward as polyps — a distinct pathway from the ciliary failure that causes rhinosinusitis.

interactions.label: An adolescent male presents with recurrent unilateral epistaxis and progressive

params.question: An adolescent male presents with recurrent unilateral epistaxis and progressive nasal obstruction. A firm mass is seen in the nasopharynx. The most appropriate next step is:

answers.text: Incisional biopsy of the mass in the outpatient clinic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NEVER biopsy a suspected juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma in clinic — the tumour is highly vascular and biopsy can cause catastrophic haemorrhage.

answers.text: A course of intranasal corticosteroid spray for six weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Corticosteroids are first-line for nasal polyps, not for a suspected angiofibroma. This mass requires imaging confirmation, not medical management.

answers.text: Contrast-enhanced CT and MRI of the nasopharynx

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction, and a nasopharyngeal mass in an adolescent male is the classic triad for juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. Contrast CT and MRI confirm the diagnosis and delineate its extent before any intervention.

answers.text: Anterior nasal packing and discharge with oral antibiotics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Packing addresses bleeding temporarily but ignores the underlying lesion. This triad demands urgent imaging to rule out juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

overallFeedback.feedback: The triad of recurrent epistaxis, nasal obstruction, and a nasopharyngeal mass in an adolescent male points to juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. The critical rule: never biopsy in clinic — confirm with contrast CT and MRI first, because the tumour is highly vascular.

Exactly right. The triad of epistaxis, obstruction, and nasopharyngeal mass in an adolescent male is classic for JNA. Imaging first, never biopsy — the vascularity of this tumour makes clinic biopsy potentially fatal.

params.question: A patient with a five-day upper respiratory tract infection was improving but suddenly worsens with high fever, purulent nasal discharge, and severe facial pain. This pattern is best described as:

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Allergic rhinosinusitis shows allergen-related fluctuation and bilateral clear discharge, not the pattern of improvement followed by sudden worsening with purulence.
Chronic rhinosinusitis requires symptoms persisting beyond twelve weeks with objective evidence on endoscopy or CT. A five-day illness does not qualify.

Correct. Double sickening — initial improvement from a viral illness followed by sudden deterioration with fever, purulence, and pain — is the classic indicator of bacterial superinfection and one of the key triggers for antibiotic therapy.

answers.text: Viral rhinosinusitis entering its peak inflammatory phase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Viral URTI symptoms typically peak at days three to five and then improve. Sudden worsening after initial improvement points to bacterial superinfection, not a late viral peak.

overallFeedback.feedback: This pattern — improvement followed by sudden worsening — is called double sickening and indicates bacterial superinfection. It is one of three triggers for antibiotic therapy, alongside symptoms persisting beyond ten days and fever above 38.5°C.
Well done. Double sickening is one of three triggers for antibiotics in acute rhinosinusitis — along with symptoms beyond ten days without improvement and fever above 38.5°C.

interactions.label: In a patient with sinusitis-related orbital complications, the presence of propt

params.question: In a patient with sinusitis-related orbital complications, the presence of proptosis with restricted eye movements can be safely managed with intravenous antibiotics alone.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Proptosis and restricted eye movements indicate disease beyond Chandler Class I. Their presence requires urgent CT and likely surgical drainage, not antibiotics alone. Medical management is safe only when there is no proptosis, eye movements are full, and vision is normal.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Any proptosis, restriction of eye movements, or visual change demands urgent CT scanning and likely surgical drainage within hours. Intravenous antibiotics alone are sufficient only for preseptal cellulitis (Chandler Class I), where there is no proptosis and eye movements are full.

params.question: A 28-year-old presents on day three of nasal congestion, mild facial pressure, and clear rhinorrhoea following an upper respiratory tract infection. She requests antibiotics. The most appropriate management is:

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Over 90% of acute rhinosinusitis is viral. At day three with mild symptoms and clear discharge, antibiotics are not indicated and prescribing them fuels antimicrobial resistance without benefit.

answers.text: Order a CT scan of the paranasal sinuses to guide treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CT is the investigation of choice for surgical planning in chronic rhinosinusitis, not for routine acute viral illness at day three.

answers.text: Advise symptomatic treatment with analgesics, saline irrigation, and short-term decongestants

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This is acute viral rhinosinusitis — day three, no severe features, no double sickening. Symptomatic management suffices. Antibiotics are warranted only after ten days without improvement, fever ≥38.5°C, or double sickening.

answers.text: Prescribe a course of oral prednisolone to reduce mucosal inflammation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Systemic corticosteroids are used as a short course in moderate-to-severe nasal polyps or chronic rhinosinusitis, not for uncomplicated acute viral illness.

overallFeedback.feedback: At day three with mild symptoms and clear discharge, this is viral rhinosinusitis. The correct approach is symptomatic treatment — analgesics, saline irrigation, and short-term decongestants. Antibiotics are appropriate only when symptoms persist beyond ten days, fever exceeds 38.5°C, or double sickening occurs.
Exactly right. Withholding antibiotics in viral rhinosinusitis is evidence-based practice. Reserve them for the three bacterial triggers: symptoms beyond ten days, fever ≥38.5°C, or double sickening.
